actual_action: Claudius authorised the Roman invasion. Aulus Plautius led a large expeditionary force into Britain in 43 CE, defeated resisting British forces and established a Roman foothold. Claudius later joined the campaign, captured Camulodunum, accepted some submissions, used force against others and ordered continued subjugation of remaining districts.
later_evidence: Cassius Dio's later narrative describes substantial armed resistance, Roman and British casualties, and continued conquest beyond the initial intervention.

Claudius returned to Rome and celebrated an elaborate triumph; the Senate granted him the title Britannicus and commemorative honours, reinforcing that conquest and prestige became major political outcomes of the campaign.

Roman rule expanded over much of Britain and lasted for centuries in many regions, bringing administrative, economic, military and cultural changes whose benefits and harms were distributed unevenly and remain historically debated.

Later resistance, including the Boudican revolt, demonstrates that Roman rule was not simply the consensual extension of an invited alliance, although individual British rulers and communities at times allied with or accommodated Rome.
outcomes: A dispute involving an exiled claimant and deserters developed into sustained territorial conquest and imperial incorporation.
Some British groups capitulated or aligned with Rome while others were defeated by force; those different responses should not be collapsed into one claim of island-wide consent.
The emperor and Roman elite gained substantial prestige from the conquest in addition to any strategic or economic benefits.
later_reviews_or_findings: The surviving literary sources are too late and partisan/literary to establish Claudius' inner motive with modern evidential confidence; the Crucible should therefore report uncertainty rather than make personal-glory motive decisive.
Later infrastructure, trade, legal or cultural effects do not by themselves establish that the initial invasion was necessary or consensual at the decision point.

This case is retained as an analogue for benevolent-imperial logic: a more capable power may produce later benefits yet still require an independently justified basis before coercively imposing rule on others.
